<reason>A wins a competitive debate through more responsive argumentation. It defended reciprocal responsibility based on sustained parental support, present need, and genuine capacity—not repayment for childhood—and explained why public guarantees need not settle cost allocation. B’s equal-income comparison and privacy objections remained substantial. However, B repeatedly understated A’s financial protections and treated the public-care guarantee, present from the opening, as a decisive new concession. A better defended the actual bounded proposal against the strongest pressure.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A directly answered the abuse-enforcement challenge with agency-borne proof, publicly funded review, admissible testimony, and no recovery under serious doubt. B correctly identified residual intrusion, but its continued claims about bare-subsistence protection and victims having to prove old wounds insufficiently engaged those safeguards.</best_rebuttal>
